docs.body: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways. To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation. prevention

docs.body: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. docs.body: A classical result for a burning droplet. The square of its diameter falls in a straight line with time. The slope is the burning rate constant.

docs.title: Burning rate constant
docs.keywords: burning rate burn rate k
docs.body: How fast the square of a droplet's diameter shrinks, in square millimetres per second. A larger value means the droplet burns away faster.

docs.title: Extinction
docs.keywords: extinguish extinguishment goes out flame out extinction limit
docs.body: The point where a flame goes out. In FLEX, extinction means the visible flame went out before the droplet was fully burned.

docs.title: Flammability limit
docs.keywords: flammability limits flammability flammable limiting oxygen index loi
docs.body: The boundary between conditions where a material burns and where it does not, for example the lowest oxygen level that still supports a flame.

docs.title: Normoxic atmosphere
docs.keywords: normoxic partial pressure oxygen partial pressure ppo2
docs.body: An atmosphere that gives the same oxygen partial pressure as sea level air, about 0.21 atm. Lower pressure with more oxygen can keep breathing normal and still make materials easier to burn.

docs.title: Diluent
docs.keywords: diluents inert gas dilution nitrogen n2
docs.body: An inert gas mixed into the atmosphere or the fuel, such as nitrogen, carbon dioxide or helium. Diluents take heat from a flame and can put it out.

docs.title: Carbon dioxide as a suppressant
docs.keywords: co2 carbon dioxide suppressant suppressants extinguisher extinguishers
docs.body: The FLEX record names carbon dioxide and helium among the gaseous fire suppressants it set out to measure. FLEX burned droplets in atmospheres with added carbon dioxide to see how well it suppresses a flame.

docs.title: Helium as a diluent
docs.keywords: helium he
docs.body: Helium carries heat away from a flame quickly. FLEX and CFI used helium in some atmospheres to study extinction and cool flames.

docs.title: PMMA
docs.keywords: acrylic plexiglass plastic plastics polymethyl methacrylate
docs.body: Polymethyl methacrylate, a clear plastic also known as acrylic. It burns steadily, so it is a standard sample in flammability tests such as BASS-II and Saffire-II.

docs.title: SIBAL fabric
docs.keywords: sibal fabric fabrics cotton cloth textile textiles fiberglass nomex
docs.body: A fabric of 75 percent cotton on a 25 percent fiberglass backing, made for flame spread tests. BASS and Saffire burned it.

docs.title: Concurrent and opposed flow
docs.keywords: concurrent opposed flame spread flow direction ventilation air flow
docs.body: Concurrent means the flame spreads in the same direction as the air flow. Opposed means it spreads against the flow. Saffire and BASS tested both.

docs.title: Smoke point
docs.keywords: smoke points soot sooting
docs.body: The flame size at which a flame starts to release soot as smoke. SPICE measured smoke points of gas jet flames in microgravity.

docs.title: Smoke aerosol
docs.keywords: smoke aerosol aerosols particles particulate smoke detector detector detectors dust
docs.body: The tiny particles and droplets that make up smoke. Their size decides whether a detector can see them. SAME and SAME-R measured them in microgravity.

docs.title: Adiabatic flame temperature
docs.keywords: tad flame temperature adiabatic
docs.body: The temperature a flame would reach if it lost no heat. It is a calculated upper value. The ACME tables list it in a column headed Tad (K).

docs.title: Evidence Coverage
docs.keywords: coverage coverage score evidence coverage score score
docs.body: EMBER's count of real flight tests near a chosen habitat atmosphere, on a scale of 0 to 100. It is not a safety rating.

docs.title: Prevention, detection and suppression
docs.keywords: prevention detection suppression pillar pillars
docs.body: The three parts of spacecraft fire safety named in the challenge statement. Prevention is about materials and ignition sources. Detection is about sensing smoke. Suppression is about putting a fire out.

docs.title: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
docs.keywords: nasa std 6001 screening test upward flame propagation material screening
docs.body: NASA's standard flammability screening test, an upward flame propagation test in normal gravity. BASS and Saffire set out to connect it with real behaviour in microgravity.

docs.title: Combustion Integrated Rack
docs.keywords: cir acme mdca hardware rack shared hardware
docs.body: A combustion laboratory rack on the ISS. It hosted the droplet experiments FLEX, FLEX-2 and CFI, and the ACME gas flame experiments.

docs.title: Microgravity Science Glovebox
docs.keywords: msg glovebox
docs.body: A sealed work volume on the ISS where crew can run small experiments by hand. BASS, BASS-II, SPICE and SLICE ran in it.

docs.title: Cygnus cargo vehicle
docs.keywords: cygnus saffire large scale fire
docs.body: An uncrewed supply ship. After it left the ISS, the Saffire experiments burned large samples inside it, which would be too risky with a crew aboard.

docs.title: Exploration atmosphere
docs.keywords: moon base lunar base rover pressurized rover lander 34 percent 8.2 psi habitat
docs.body: A cabin atmosphere with more oxygen at lower pressure than sea level air, planned so crews can start spacewalks faster. NASA reports give 34 percent oxygen at 8.2 psi. The challenge statement expects 30 percent or more at 10.2 psi or less for a Moon Base.

Evidence Coverage near this atmosphere is 100 out of 100: prevention 100, detection 100, suppression 100. Tests within one unit of distance: 1093 (119 aerosol, 618 gas, 127 liquid, 229 solid). The score counts nearby flight tests. It is not a safety rating.

It is not a safety rating.

docs.body: Mars surface habitat: 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi, Mars gravity 0.38 g. Source: The same exploration atmosphere, with Mars gravity. Evidence Coverage near this atmosphere is 67 out of 100: prevention 60, detection 58, suppression 84. Tests within one unit of distance: 24 (15 gas, 9 liquid). The score counts nearby flight tests. It is not a safety rating.

docs.body: Spacesuit: 100% oxygen at 4.3 psi, any gravity. Source: Challenge statement. Evidence Coverage near this atmosphere is 0 out of 100: prevention 0, detection 0, suppression 0. Tests within one unit of distance: 0. The score counts nearby flight tests. It is not a safety rating.

docs.title: What the Evidence Coverage score means
docs.body: Evidence Coverage measures how much real flight evidence sits close to a chosen habitat atmosphere, on a scale of 0 to 100. It is not a safety rating. Each test gets a weight that falls with its distance from the habitat: 4 points of oxygen is one unit of distance and about 25 percent in pressure is one unit. A test whose oxygen or pressure is assumed counts at half weight. For each pillar the weights are summed into an effective number of nearby tests N, and coverage is 100 × (1 − exp(−N ÷ 10)). The overall score is 0.4 × prevention plus 0.3 × detection plus 0.3 × suppression. Fundamentals tests count toward each pillar at a weight of 0.3. The constants are design choices by the team.

docs.title: How investigations are ranked
docs.body: The relevance ranking is a transparent heuristic. Each investigation gets a score out of 100 from four parts: how many of its tests sit near the chosen atmosphere (weight 0.45), its fuel type (0.25, with solid materials highest), whether its pillar matches the focus pillar (0.20), and how much test data it has (0.10). Every ranked card shows the four parts under the heading Why this rank.

docs.title: The d-squared law
docs.body: The d-squared law says the square of a burning droplet's diameter falls in a straight line with time: d(t)² = d0² − K × t. K is the burning rate constant. The burn time to extinction is (d0² − dExt²) ÷ K. EMBER checks this against the FLEX table. Source: Dietrich and co-authors, Droplet Combustion Experiments Aboard the International Space Station, 2014.

docs.title: Declared assumptions
docs.body: Some PSI tables do not state an atmosphere. For 6 investigations EMBER assumes cabin air, 21% oxygen at one atmosphere: PSI-26, PSI-102, PSI-101, PSI-47, PSI-107, PSI-106. That covers 722 tests. Assumed values are drawn as hollow marks, marked as assumed in every table, and counted at half weight in the coverage score. They are never presented as measured.

docs.title: Limits of EMBER
docs.body: The Evidence Coverage score counts evidence and is not a safety rating. The ranking is a heuristic. The PSI test tables are summaries and not the full datasets. Assumed atmospheres are marked. EMBER does not say that any material, atmosphere or habitat is safe or unsafe. PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion tests, so nothing here describes how a flame behaves on the Moon or Mars.

docs.title: Combustion Integrated Rack with the ACME insert
docs.body: Hardware family: Combustion Integrated Rack with the ACME insert. Gaseous fuels on the ISS. Six ACME experiments shared this hardware. 6 investigations shared it: ACME Flame Design (PSI-10), ACME BRE (PSI-20), ACME CLD Flame (PSI-21), ACME E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22), ACME s-Flame (PSI-23), ACME CFI-G (PSI-159).

docs.title: Combustion Integrated Rack with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus
docs.body: Hardware family: Combustion Integrated Rack with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus. Liquid fuel droplets on the ISS. 3 investigations shared it: CFI (PSI-39), FLEX-2 (PSI-68), FLEX (PSI-69).

docs.title: Microgravity Science Glovebox with the SPICE flow duct
docs.body: Hardware family: Microgravity Science Glovebox with the SPICE flow duct. Solid and gaseous fuels in a small flow duct on the ISS. 4 investigations shared it: BASS-II (PSI-25), BASS (PSI-26), SLICE (PSI-106), SPICE (PSI-107).

docs.title: Cygnus cargo vehicle
docs.body: Hardware family: Cygnus cargo vehicle. Large solid samples burned in an uncrewed cargo vehicle after it left the ISS. 3 investigations shared it: Saffire-I (PSI-98), Saffire-II (PSI-99), Saffire-III (PSI-100).

docs.title: Smoke and aerosol instruments
docs.body: Hardware family: Smoke and aerosol instruments. Smoke and dust particle measurements on the ISS. 3 investigations shared it: DAFT and DAFT-2 (PSI-47), SAME-R (PSI-101), SAME (PSI-102).

docs.title: Ground and modelling studies
docs.body: Hardware family: Ground and modelling studies. Analysis, simulation or laboratory work on the ground that uses PSI flight data. 5 investigations shared it: SPICE data analysis (PSI-60), BASS flame spread modelling (PSI-62), SAME smoke simulation (PSI-115), Cool flame CFD analysis (PSI-117), Cool flame counterflow study (PSI-142).

docs.title: Apollo 1, 1967
docs.body: Apollo 1, 1967. On 27 January 1967 three astronauts lost their lives when a fire swept through the Apollo 1 command module during a preflight test. NASA's review found that the pure oxygen atmosphere let the fire spread quickly, and NASA then restricted combustible materials in the spacecraft and replaced the hatch with one that opens in three seconds. This is context from a NASA page (NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance, Apollo 1). It is not test data.

docs.title: Apollo 13, 1970
docs.body: Apollo 13, 1970. On the third day of the mission, oxygen tank number two blew up, which led to the failure of tank number one and ended the plan to land on the Moon. For later missions engineers redesigned the oxygen tank system and sheathed all electrical wiring in stainless steel. This is context from a NASA page (NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance, Apollo 13). It is not test data.

docs.title: Fire aboard Mir, 1997
docs.body: Fire aboard Mir, 1997. On 24 February 1997 a fire ignited in an oxygen generating system aboard the space station Mir, with six crew members aboard. The flame lasted several minutes, cut off access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles and filled the modules with smoke before the crew put it out. This is context from a NASA page (NASA History, 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir). It is not test data.

docs.title: Lighter air tanks for firefighters
docs.body: Lighter air tanks for firefighters. NASA's Johnson Space Center and Scott Aviation developed lightweight air tanks for firefighters. The backpack system weighs 20 pounds for a 30 minute air supply, which is 13 pounds less than conventional firefighting tanks. This is context from a NASA page (NASA Spinoff, Fireman's Air Tanks). It is not test data.

docs.title: A detector that tells smoke from dust
docs.body: A detector that tells smoke from dust. A fire detector first used in space shuttle orbiters samples the air for combustion particles and can tell them apart from other matter such as dust. That makes it less susceptible to false alarms. This is context from a NASA page (NASA Spinoff, Fire Detector). It is not test data.

docs.title: Better protective gear for firefighters
docs.body: Better protective gear for firefighters. Project FIRES, sponsored by NASA and the U.S. Fire Administration, applied lightweight, fire-resistant and heat-protective materials first developed for astronauts' space suits to firefighter gear. Its goal was to curb injuries and fatalities among firefighters. This is context from a NASA page (NASA Spinoff, New Technology for the Fire Attire). It is not test data.
